title: Who will fill Nancy Pelosi's congressional seat?

Who will fill Nancy Pelosi's congressional seat? - ABC7 San Francisco 
 24/7 Live San Francisco East Bay South Bay Peninsula North Bay Live POLITICS 
 Live election updates: California voters reject Prop 40, a measure to tax the wealth of billionaires 
 Stream local breaking news and original programming, live 24/7, from ABC7 Bay Area. Last updated: Tuesday, November 10, 2026 3:38AM GMT Share SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- Election Day has passed and results are continuing to roll in across California and right here in the Bay Area.
 Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who ran on his decades of experience in public office, will take over from California Gov. Gavin Newsom as the next governor of the nation's most populous state.
 Locally, State Sen. Scott Wiener was leading San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan in the early returns from Tuesday's election to replace House Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi in Congress.
 In the East Bay, Aisha Wahab was ahead of Melissa Hernandez in the race to replace Eric Swalwell in California's 14th Congressional District based on early returns Tuesday night.

 Who will fill Nancy Pelosi's congressional seat? 
 San Francisco voters are preparing to elect someone other than Nancy Pelosi to Congress for the first time in nearly four decades, with state Sen. Scott Wiener and Supervisor Connie Chan competing to succeed the former House speaker.
 With Pelosi backing Chan and other prominent Democrats, including former Rep. Katie Porter, supporting Wiener, the race will determine not only who represents San Francisco in Congress but also what kind of Democrat voters want to succeed Pelosi.
 Both Democracts support expanding health care access and federal investment in housing but they differ sharply over regulating artificial intelligence, addressing the housing shortage and taxing billionairses.
 Chan is a labor-backed progressive endorsed by Pelosi calling for stricter oversight of AI, including
 Chan, a labor-backed progressive endorsed by Pelosi, is calling for stricter oversight of AI, including a moratorium on new AI data centers until stronger federal safeguards are established, while Wiener favors safety standards that balance regulation with technological innovation.
 On housing, Wiener wants to use federal incentives to accelerate construction and expand social housing, while Chan emphasizes affordability requirements, rental assistance and keeping existing residents housed.
 Both candidates support moving toward Medicare for All, but Chan backs Proposition 40, a proposed one-time 5% wealth tax on California billionaires, while Wiener opposes using a one-time tax to pay for ongoing health care expenses.
 The candidates also differ over corporate campaign money and U.S. military assistance to Israel, reflecting broader disagreements over the direction of the Democratic Party.
 With Pelosi backing Chan and other prominent Democrats, including former Rep. Katie Porter, supporting Wiener, the race will determine not only who represents San Francisco in Congress but also what kind of Democrat voters want to succeed Pelosi.

 Wahab, Hernandez look to fill Swalwell's seat for full 2-year term 
 California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez are vying for California District 14's seat after it was vacated by former Rep. Eric Swalwell following sexual assault allegations.
 Swalwell, a Democrat who was running for California governor, ended his campaign and resigned from Congress in April after he was accused of sexual assault and harassment. He has denied the allegations.
 Wahab defeated Hernandez in the state's 14th Congressional District special election in August to serve the rest of Swalwell's term, which ends in January.
 Now the two are hoping to serve the next full two-year term.
 Wahab has championed housing affordability and access. She also wrote a 2023 bill to ban caste-based discrimination, which drew national attention. Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed it, saying civil rights protections already outlaw such discrimination.
 Wahab became the first Afghan American elected to public office in the U.S. when she won a Hayward City Council seat in 2018. She is the first Afghan American to serve in Congress.
 By Lindsay Whitehurst Nov 02, 2026, 5:58 PM GMT 
 Trump administration appeals to Supreme Court in push to sideline 20,000 California mail ballots 
 President Donald Trump's administration appealed to the Supreme Court on Monday in its push to sideline thousands of disputed California mail ballots the day before the pivotal midterm elections.
 The emergency appeal came after an appeals court rejected the request to set aside some 20,000 ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens.
 The federal government says those ballots should not be counted until the voters' status can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
 The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare.
 A district court judge forcefully denied the Justice Department's request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens in the Nov. 3 midterm elections to determine control of Congress.
 The Justice Department asked the high court for a "limited injunction" that would direct California to "stop commingling suspected illegal ballots with legal ones" while the case continues to play out.
 Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. All of the state's roughly 23 million registered voters are mailed a ballot. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed.
 By Jaime Geary and Gabriella Guerrieri Nov 02, 2026, 5:58 PM GMT 
 Contra Costa Co. denies Trump administration's request for voter information 
 Times are tense for local officials under pressure from the Trump administration to restrict voting in Tuesday's election - and some are pushing back.
 On Wednesday, Contra Costa County's Office of the Clerk-Recorder-Registrar denied a request for the personal information of hundreds of Contra Costa County voters. The administration asked for Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers and voter registration data before the midterm election Tuesday.
 The administration's Department of Justice claims the records belong to noncitizens who are "likely aliens," and requested any votes from those records not be counted until further notice. United States residents must be citizens to register to vote.
 In the county's rejection letter, county counsel Thomas Geiger said the registrar would not disclose the records information because "it would be unlawful and a breach of the voters' trust."
 On Oct. 23, U.S. government officials showed up to hand-deliver papers to Contra Costa County clerk-recorder-registrar Kristin Connelly, who manages the county's elections office. Connelly directed the officials to Geiger.
 The papers demanded the county turn over and invalidate 407 voter records within 48 hours or face legal action.
 "It's unenforceable. It's... yeah, it was threatening," Connelly said.
 The DOJ's lawsuit came just days before Election Day, a high-profile event with much at stake for federal, state and local contests.
 Registrar of voter offices like Connelly's are already deep in the process of counting and sorting ballots that have been collected and turned in early. Roughly 100 volunteers are at work every day, unpacking mail-in votes to pre-count the votes before the official tally begins Tuesday.
 "I'm wanting my staff to absolutely stay focused on the election we're in the middle of so that they can be processing ballots, and you'll see all of this today, that we're very busy," said Connelly on Wednesday during a tour of the facilities where ballots get sorted and scanned.
 Contra Costa County is one of several California counties the DOJ is suing in an attempt to invalidate 20,000 voter records they say belong to noncitizens.
 U.S. District Court Judge David Carter dismissed the DOJ's case on Wednesday. At the hearing, Carter said California law allows up to 30 days for the election to be certified, and questioned whether the department needed the records immediately.
 The DOJ immediately appealed that decision, and is escalating threats to include criminal subpoenas. In October, the agency threatened Los Angeles County they would criminally prosecute election workers who "knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens."
 Now, the DOJ has issued subpoenas to county election workers across the state, asking them to appear in court on Wednesday, the day after the midterm election, to testify as part of a criminal investigation.
 Some observers are alarmed by the threatening nature of the demands.
 David Becker, founder of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, worked with the DOJ on voting for seven years. Becker said the Trump DOJ's actions reveal "a broad, ongoing pattern of attempted election interference by federal officials."
 The DOJ is apparently using data from the Department of Homeland Security to identify registered voters they say do not have citizenship status. Becker said the DHS has not disclosed how they gathered this information.
 "The DOJ doesn't even seem to be aware of exactly what was done with that data and how it came about," Becker said.
 In his letter to the DOJ, Geiger said the Department of Justice had not given Contra Costa County "information about the source or accuracy of the allegations regarding these voters."
 In July, the DOJ said there were roughly 190,000 non-citizen voters in California, a much higher number than the DOJ's current tally of 20,000. Either way, it is a small fraction of the 23 million registered voters in the state.
 "Where did those other 170,000 go? Nobody knows." Becker said.
 The Trump administration has repeatedly requested voter records since taking office. In July of last year, the Trump administration demanded a list of all California voters plus their citizenship status and personally identifiable information.
 California denied that request, and is one of 30 states to do so. At least 48 states and Washington, D.C. have received requests for complete registration lists.
 Connelly said the controversy has created confusion and concern among voters, and she is fielding questions from citizens about whether elections are secure.
 As a precaution, her office is hiring private security for the election buildings during the entire election process, replacing Contra Costa County sheriff's deputies who would patrol the building on election night only.
 "I'm trying to engage in the best practices to keep everybody safe," Connelly said.
